scripts.hook: Is expecting the worst pessimism, or protection?
scripts.hook_b: Seneca's friend watched his whole city burn in one night.
cards: Is expecting the worst pessimism, or protection?
One reading: you're ruining today with a disaster that hasn't happened.
The other: you're making sure it can't ambush you.
When Lyon burned in one night, Seneca wrote to a friend from there.
His point: what has happened to anyone can happen to you.
If it ends in a feeling, it's dread. If it ends in a plan, it's protection.
Which one is yours? Answer below.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Quote card in Playfair italic.

source.author: Seneca
source.verified_at: Letter 91 (to Liberalis, on the fire at Lyon) paraphrased on screen and in the caption; no verbatim quote used

scripts.caption:
In AD 64 Lyon burned to the ground in a single night. Seneca wrote to his friend Liberalis, who came from there, and his advice wasn't comfort. It was: nothing should be unexpected. Whatever has happened to anyone can happen to you, so think it through once, calmly, before it does. (Letters 91, in our words.)

That's the line between dread and protection. Dread rehearses the feeling and stops. Protection rehearses the event and ends in a plan: what you'd do first, who you'd call, what you'd still have.

Same thought. Different ending.

Send this to the friend who rehearses disasters in the shower.

Dread or plan?

— Moodius

scripts.hook: A slave in Nero's Rome walked with a limp. Nobody knows why.
scripts.hook_b: He was owned by a man at Nero's court. Watch what happened.
cards: A slave in Nero's Rome walked with a limp. Nobody knows why.
Born into slavery around AD 50. Even his name means "acquired".
His owner was Nero's secretary. Still a slave, he was sent to philosophy lectures.

What you control.
What you don't.
Taught to a man who owned nothing.
Freed after Nero died. Taught in Rome until an emperor threw the philosophers out.
He opened a school in a small Greek town. Students came from across the empire.
Facts: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Epictetus" · Part 1 of 3
Part 1 of 3. Full story Sunday. Heard of him? Answer below.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Quote card in Playfair italic.

source.author: Epictetus (biography)
source.verified_at: hook-system.md arc 1 facts (SEP): born 50s CE Hierapolis; enslaved to Epaphroditus; limp of unknown cause; studied under Musonius Rufus; banished under Domitian; school at Nicopolis

scripts.caption:
Part 1 of 3. He was born into slavery around AD 50 in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey. Even the name we have for him, Epictetus, just means "acquired". His owner, Epaphroditus, was Nero's secretary, and while still enslaved he was allowed to study under Musonius Rufus, the leading Stoic teacher in Rome. He walked with a limp; ancient writers disagree about why.

Freed after Nero's death, he taught in Rome until Domitian banished philosophers from the city, then opened a school in Nicopolis, a small town in western Greece. Students travelled from across the empire to hear a former slave explain what is and isn't in your power.

Part 2 on Friday at 5. The full story is Sunday's carousel.

Send this to the friend who thinks philosophy was invented by comfortable people.

Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Epictetus"; Arrian's Discourses.

Heard of him?

— Moodius

scripts.hook: What did you agree to this week just to keep the peace?
scripts.hook_b: A former slave had one question for people who say yes too fast.
cards: What did you agree to this week just to keep the peace?
The meeting you didn't want. The favour you can't afford.
Epictetus had a question for it. He'd been property once, so he meant it.
“…how much you are worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself; for men sell themselves at various prices.”
Epictetus, Discourses 1.2, tr. George Long (public domain)
He said this as a free man. He knew exactly what being sold cost.
Say yes if you like. Just know what you're selling.
Name the price. Answer below. Part 2 of 3.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Quote card in Playfair italic.

source.author: Epictetus
source.verified_at: Standard Ebooks, Discourses Book I ch. 2 (Long), checked 8 Nov 2026

scripts.caption:
Part 2 of 3. Epictetus, who had been enslaved for the first part of his life, told his students that the real question before any decision is what you'd sell yourself for. Discourses 1.2 (tr. George Long): "it is you who know yourself, how much you are worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself; for men sell themselves at various prices."

He isn't against saying yes. He's against not knowing the price. The meeting you sat through, the favour you'll resent by Thursday, the "sure, no problem" that cost you a Sunday: each one was a sale. Some are worth it. Know which.

Send this to the friend who says yes before the sentence is finished.

Name the price?

— Moodius

scripts.hook: A former slave's three-step test for how free you are.
scripts.hook_b: How free are you, honestly? Epictetus had a three-step test.
cards: A former slave's three-step test for how free you are.
Not free as in money or borders. Free as in who's running you.
When something goes wrong, who do you blame?

Step 1 · other people
Step 2 · yourself
Step 3 · nobody
“…and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself.”
Epictetus, Enchiridion 5, tr. George Long (public domain)
Not blaming yourself isn't letting yourself off. It's dropping the whole trial.
He's not saying nothing's your fault. He's saying blame is a habit, and habits can be dropped.
Which step are you on? Answer below. Part 3 of 3.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Quote card in Playfair italic.

source.author: Epictetus
source.verified_at: Standard Ebooks, Enchiridion V (Long), checked 8 Nov 2026

scripts.caption:
Part 3 of 3. Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 (tr. George Long): "It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition; it is the act of one who has begun to be instructed, to lay the blame on himself; and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself."

Three steps. Most of us live on step one, visit step two on bad nights, and assume step three means not caring. It doesn't. It means the event happened, your opinion about it is yours to set, and there's no trial to hold. That's what a man who had been owned meant by free.

Full story in Sunday's carousel.

Send this to the friend who's been prosecuting themselves since Tuesday.

Which step?

— Moodius

scripts.hook: You spent today guessing what one person thinks of you.
scripts.hook_b: Marcus Aurelius had a rule about guessing what people think of you.
cards: You spent today guessing what one person thinks of you.
The slow reply. The tone in the meeting.
You've run the scene nine times. They've run it zero.

A day of your attention,
spent inside
someone else's head.
Marcus described the mind he was aiming for. One habit was almost absent from it:
“…imagining what another says, or does, or thinks.”
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 3.4, tr. George Long (public domain)
Count the guesses. Then ask: what's actually mine to do here?
Send this to the one who's overthinking a text right now.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Quote card in Playfair italic.

source.author: Marcus Aurelius
source.verified_at: Standard Ebooks, Meditations Book III (Long), checked 8 Nov 2026

scripts.caption:
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 3.4 (tr. George Long), describing the person he wanted to be: one who is "not often, nor yet without great necessity and for the general interest, imagining what another says, or does, or thinks."

Not never. Not often. He knew the pull of it: the slow reply, the half-second face in the meeting, the like that didn't come. He also knew where that attention goes: into a head you can't see, away from the one thing you can actually act on.

Tonight, count today's guesses. Then ask the only question with an answer: what's mine to do here?

Send this to the friend who's overthinking a text right now.

How many guesses?

— Moodius

scripts.hook: Everyone has a theory of what a good person is.
scripts.hook_b: The emperor of Rome learned his philosophy from a former slave.
cards: Everyone has a theory of what a good person is.
Marcus Aurelius had one too. He also had an empire, a plague and a war.
“No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.”
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 10.16, tr. George Long (public domain)
Epictetus taught him that, through his notes: stop describing the good life, do a piece of it.
Today's piece can be small. One kept promise. One honest sentence.
Whose is right? Answer below. Full Epictetus story: today's carousel.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Quote card in Playfair italic.

source.author: Marcus Aurelius
source.verified_at: Standard Ebooks, Meditations Book X (Long), checked 8 Nov 2026

scripts.caption:
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 10.16 (tr. George Long): "No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such."

He wrote it to himself, in a notebook nobody was meant to read, after years of arguing the theory. The man whose lecture notes taught him Stoicism, Epictetus, had been a slave; his version of the same idea was that philosophy is shown in what you do, not what you can explain. (Today's carousel has the whole story.)

The piece you do today can be small. A promise kept. A sentence you'd been avoiding.

Send this to the friend who can describe the good life in detail.

Whose is right?

— Moodius

scripts.hook: Listen to how you explain your bad day.
scripts.hook_b: Epictetus had a one-sentence test you can hear in anyone's bad day.
cards: Listen to how you explain your bad day.
"The train, then my manager, then the weather." Who's in the sentence?
Epictetus listened for the same thing in his students.
“The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is this: he expects all advantage and all harm from himself.”
Epictetus, Enchiridion 48, tr. George Long (public domain)
Same bad day. But now the sentence has you in it, and that's the only part you can change.
Say your sentence out loud. Who's in it? Answer below.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Quote card in Playfair italic.

source.author: Epictetus
source.verified_at: Standard Ebooks, Enchiridion XLVIII (Long), checked 8 Nov 2026

scripts.caption:
Epictetus, Enchiridion 48 (tr. George Long): the uninstructed person "never expects from himself profit nor harm, but from externals", while "the condition and characteristic of a philosopher is this: he expects all advantage and all harm from himself."

You can hear it in one sentence. "The train, then my manager, then the weather" has no one in it who can do anything. "I left late, I didn't push back, I forgot the coat" is the same day, and it's miserable too, but now it has you in it, and you're the only part that can change by tomorrow.

Not blame. Location.

Send this to the friend whose bad days are always somebody else's.

Who's in your sentence?

— Moodius
